extracted.intended_audience: petitioners, patent owners, and patent practitioners participating in PTAB post-grant review (PGR) proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and decision-making criteria the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB) applies when deciding whether to institute a post-grant review (PGR) under the AIA, including statutory thresholds, discretion doctrines (§325(d), Fintiv), claim construction, written description, indefiniteness, obviousness (Graham/KSR), and related evidentiary considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institution standard under 35 U.S.C. § 324(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Institution of a post-grant review is authorized by statute when 'the information presented in the petition . . . would demonstrate that it is more likely than not that at least 1 of the claims challenged in the petition is unpatentable.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the 'more likely than not' threshold on the basis of the Petition, Preliminary Response, and the evidence of record. Institution is discretionary but the statutory threshold must be met before instituting trial. Consider all presented grounds and evidence to determine whether Petitioner would likely prevail on at least one challenged claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: § 325(d) two-part framework
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board uses a two-part framework: (1) whether the same or substantially the same prior art or arguments previously were presented to the Office; and (2) if so, whether the petitioner has demonstrated that the Office erred in a manner material to the patentability of the challenged claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the same or substantially the same art/arguments were before the Examiner, institution may be denied; but petitioner can overcome §325(d) by showing material Examiner error. See Advanced Bionics precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Becton, Dickinson non-exclusive factors for § 325(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-exclusive factors to guide application of the §325(d) framework: (a) the similarities and material differences between the asserted art and the prior art involved during examination; (b) the cumulative nature of the asserted art and the prior art evaluated during examination; (c) the extent to which the asserted art was evaluated during examination, including whether the prior art was the basis for rejection; (d) the extent of the overlap between the arguments made during examination and the manner in which Petitioner relies on the prior art or Patent Owner distinguishes the prior art; (e) whether Petitioner has pointed out sufficiently how the Examiner erred in its evaluation of the asserted prior art; and (f) the extent to which additional evidence and facts presented in the Petition warrant reconsideration of the prior art or arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess (a), (b), (d) first to determine whether the same or substantially same art/arguments were presented, and if so evaluate (c), (e), (f) to determine whether the petitioner has shown a material error by the Office. Factors are non-exclusive and considered holistically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fintiv factors for discretionary denial due to parallel litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: When a parallel district-court litigation exists, consider the six Fintiv factors: (1) whether the court granted a stay or evidence exists that one may be granted if a proceeding is instituted; (2) proximity of the court's trial date to the Board's projected statutory deadline for a final written decision; (3) investment in the parallel proceeding by the court and the parties; (4) overlap between issues raised in the Petition and in the parallel litigation; (5) whether the petitioner and the defendant in the parallel litigation are the same party; and (6) other circumstances that impact the Board's exercise of discretion, including the merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh factors holistically to decide whether denying institution would better serve efficiency and integrity. Individual factors can favor or oppose denial; the Board examines them in context (e.g., stay absent is neutral; substantial overlap and same parties weigh toward denial; strong merits can weigh against denial).

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of ordinary skill in the art (PHOSITA/POSITA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define the person of ordinary skill in the art for evaluating obviousness, written description, and claim construction; parties' proposed definitions (e.g., bachelor’s degree in mechanical engineering plus 2–3 years experience vs. degree and 3–5 years product development experience) may differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board may adopt one party's proposed level if differences do not affect decision. Evidence of level of skill is usually found in the prior art references themselves. Parties may submit briefing at trial to argue adoption of one definition over another if it affects outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction standard in post-grant review
rubrics_metrics.description: In a post-grant review, claims are construed using the same claim construction standard as in civil actions under 35 U.S.C. 282(b): 'in accordance with the ordinary and customary meaning of such claim as understood by one of ordinary skill in the art and the prosecution history pertaining to the patent.' (37 C.F.R. § 42.200(b))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no party identifies terms requiring construction, the Board need not construe any term at institution. Construction follows intrinsic evidence (specification and prosecution history) and PHOSITA understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement (possession standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'A specification that "reasonably conveys to those skilled in the art that the inventor had possession of the claimed subject matter as of the filing date" has adequate written description.' (citing Novartus/Ariad)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply an objective inquiry into the four corners of the specification from the PHOSITA perspective. The written description inquiry asks whether the skilled reader would recognize that what is claimed corresponds to what was described. It is distinct from enablement (i.e., not about proof that the invention works). Examples: the Board may find a disclosure of a specific embodiment (e.g., magnetic quick-connect) can support claims to a broader 'quick release connector' if a PHOSITA would understand equivalent connectors were known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefiniteness standard (Nautilus reasonable certainty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Nautilus, a patent is invalid for indefiniteness if its claims, read in light of the specification and prosecution history, fail to inform, with reasonable certainty, those skilled in the art about the scope of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terms of degree (e.g., 'substantially cylindrical') are not inherently indefinite; the court/Board must determine whether the patent provides some standard for measuring the degree. Extrinsic evidence and the skilled artisan's understanding (and specification examples) can supply sufficient guidance to avoid indefiniteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness framework (Graham/KSR)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply Graham's four factual inquiries: (1) determine scope and content of the prior art; (2) ascertain differences between the prior art and the claims; (3) resolve the level of ordinary skill in the art; (4) consider objective evidence (secondary considerations) indicating obviousness or non-obviousness. KSR adds that combination of familiar elements per known methods is likely obvious when it yields predictable results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivation-to-combine is flexible: any need or problem known in the field that is addressed by the patent can provide a reason for combining elements. Courts/Board may rely on inferences a POSITA would make; the combination need not be the best option, only a suitable option, and a reasonable expectation of success supports obviousness findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation-to-combine and reasonable expectation of success principles
rubrics_metrics.description: A POSITA may be motivated to combine references when a known technique used to improve one device would be recognized to improve similar devices; the Board considers whether a POSITA would have had a reasonable expectation of success in making the combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analysis is fact-specific and may rely on expert declarations. It is sufficient that there be a known problem and a technique in the prior art addressing it; precise teachings directed to the specific subject matter are not required. Evidence that references have compatible systems (e.g., similar motor and drive systems) supports motivation and expectation-of-success findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of 'material error' for § 325(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: An example of a material error is misapprehending or overlooking specific teachings of the relevant prior art where those teachings impact patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the Examiner was aware of a reference but did not identify its pertinence or rely on it in a rejection, that can weigh against exercising discretion to deny institution under §325(d). Demonstrating such an error supports institution even if the same references were presented during prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight of new evidence under Becton, Dickinson factor (f)
rubrics_metrics.description: Factor (f) considers the extent to which additional evidence and facts presented in the Petition warrant reconsideration of the prior art or arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New evidence (e.g., expert declarations) not presented to the Examiner can be probative and weigh against denial under §325(d) by showing grounds and combinations not previously considered. The Board evaluates probative value of such evidence in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a single disclosed example can support broader generic claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Written description may be adequate even if the specification provides only a single working example, provided the skilled reader would understand the broader generic claim (i.e., the inventor's contribution is characterized sufficiently). Case law: Capon, Alcon, Reiffin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board distinguishes written description from enablement: it's not necessary to demonstrate every permutation of a generic claim if the effect is sufficiently demonstrated to characterize a generic invention and a PHOSITA would recognize equivalents or known alternatives (e.g., multiple types of 'quick release connectors').
